Learning Objectives
Review the pathophysiology of Charcot arthropathy of the foot and ankle.
Evaluate and diagnose a patient with Charcot arthropathy.
Differentiate Charcot arthropathy from infection.
Review the major methods of nonsurgical management for Charcot arthropathy.
Outline the surgical indications for, treatment options for, surgical outcomes of, and potential
complications of Charcot arthropathy.
Pathophysiology, Etiology, and Epidemiology
The pathogenesis of Charcot arthropathy of the ankle has been explained using two major
theories.

The neurotraumatic theory attributes bony destruction to loss of pain sensation and
proprioception in combination with repetitive and mechanical trauma.
The neurovascular theory suggests that joint destruction is secondary to an autonomic
stimulated vascular reflex, causing hyperemia and periarticular osteopenia.
Occurs in 1% to 1.5% of patients with diabetes mellitus
Occurs in 7.5% of patients with diabetes mellitus and neuropathy; of those, 9% to 35% have
bilateral involvement.

Pathophysiology, Etiology, and Epidemiology
No unifying theory has established the pathophysiologic process underlying Charcot
arthropathy of the foot and ankle. Two major theories provide models for
understanding.1
The first theory is the neurotraumatic model. This model suggests that Charcot
arthropathy essentially is an exaggerated overuse injury. Specifically, insensate joints are
subject to repetitive microtrauma or a single major traumatic event. This trauma leads to
degenerative joint disease. Poor sensation prohibits the patient from adopting normal
protective mechanisms and seeking medical attention before destruction becomes
irreversible.
The second theory is the neurovascular model. This model suggests that autonomic
dysfunction causes increased blood flow via arteriovenous shunting. This increased
blood flow results in resorption of bone and localized osteoporosis, which predisposes
patients to articular fracture. In support of this theory, bone turnover markers are
elevated in patients with Charcot arthropathy. In addition, bone density analyses have
confirmed localized osteopenia.
Newer models emphasize the role of inflammatory cytokines, such as interleukin-1 and
tumor necrosis factor alpha.2,3 These factors are believed to facilitate the
overexpression of nuclear factor kappa B, which stimulates differentiation and
maturation of osteoclasts, contributing to osteopenia and, in patients with neuropathy,
increasing the risk of periarticular fracture4,5 and uncontrolled degenerative disease.

Overall, Charcot arthropathy is much more common in patients with diabetes mellitus
than patients without diabetes mellitus, occurring in 1% to 1.5% of patients with diabetes
mellitus. Charcot arthropathy occurs in 7.5% of patients with diabetes mellitus and
neuropathy, of whom 9% to 35% have bilateral involvement.
Evaluation and Diagnosis
Patient History
Charcot arthropathy of the ankle most commonly occurs in patients with diabetes mellitus;
however, it can occur in patients with lower extremity neuropathy from any cause.
The most common presentation is a hot, swollen ankle.
Pain is present in approximately one-half of patients.
The patient history may include an inciting traumatic event.

Patient History
Acute Charcot arthropathy manifests as a hot and swollen foot or ankle.1 A
misconception is that the condition typically is painless; however, pain is thought to be
present in approximately one-half of patients with Charcot arthropathy and typically is
worse in those with earlier stages of neuropathy. Thorough questioning may reveal a
history of an inciting traumatic event.
Most commonly, Charcot arthropathy occurs in patients with diabetes mellitus; however,
it can occur in patients with lower extremity neuropathy from any cause.6,7 Patients
typically will have a hot, swollen ankle that may mimic signs of soft-tissue and bony
infection.8
In patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus, Charcot arthropathy typically occurs in
individuals in their forties, after a mean duration of diabetes mellitus of approximately
20 years.9 In patients with type 2 diabetes, Charcot arthropathy typically occurs

individuals in their fifties, after a mean duration of diabetes mellitus of approximately 5
to 10 years.
Physical Examination
Physical examination findings of Charcot arthropathy of the ankle are best understood in
terms of the Eichenholtz classification.
Stage 0 (acute): hyperemia of the foot with increased warmth and swelling
Stage I (fragmentation): continued warmth and swelling, ligamentous laxity
Stage II (coalescence): decreased warmth and swelling
Stage III (reconstruction): absence of inflammation, stable on physical examination
Classically, distal pulses are exaggerated or bounding.
Early Charcot arthropathy often is misdiagnosed as infection.
Normal white blood cell count and lack of fever favor Charcot arthropathy over infection.
Dependent rubor—evidenced by resolution of warmth, redness, and swelling with elevation
—favors Charcot arthropathy over infection.
In patients with diabetes mellitus, blood glucose level is elevated in those with infection;
therefore, a normal blood glucose level favors Charcot arthropathy over infection.

Physical Examination
Progression of Charcot arthropathy follows a clinical and radiographic pattern defined by
Eichenholtz1,10,11 (Table 1; Resource 1). In terms of physical examination findings,
Eichenholtz stage 0 refers to marked swelling and erythema that may at first elicit
suspicion of soft-tissue or bony infection, particularly in patients with diabetes mellitus.
Pulses often are exaggerated or bounding during this phase, potentially consistent with
the neurovascular theory of pathogenesis of Charcot arthropathy.

Reproduced with permission from van der Ven A, Chapman CB, Bowker JH: Charcot
neuroarthropathy of the foot and ankle. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2009;17(9):562-571.
Stage I is the fragmentation phase. On physical examination, the foot remains
edematous and warm and often displays an increase in ligamentous laxity. Stage II is the
coalescent, or early healing, phase. Edema and warmth decrease as the inflammation
resolves and bony fragments begin to reunite. Stage III is the reconstruction phase, in
which bony union is achieved. On physical examination, this phase is evidenced by
resolution of inflammation and achievement of a stable (but often deformed) foot and
ankle.
A simple method of distinguishing early Charcot arthropathy from infection involves
elevating the leg and assessing for a decrease in erythema.12 The erythema of Charcot
arthropathy is dependent, meaning that it resolves with elevation; conversely, the
erythema of infection will persist. In addition, in patients with diabetes mellitus, blood
glucose levels increase substantially during acute infection. Therefore, normal blood
glucose levels in a patient with diabetes mellitus supports Charcot arthropathy over
infection. Patients with Charcot arthropathy tend to have an absence of systemic signs of
infection, such as leukocytosis and fever; however, these signs may be unreliable in
patients with diabetes mellitus and a decreased immune response. Accordingly,
although complete blood count results often are normal or only slightly elevated in
patients with an infection, erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein level
are more likely to be sensitive to infection and may help to differentiate infection from
Charcot arthropathy.
Imaging Studies
Plain Radiography
Similar to physical examination findings, the radiographic findings of Charcot arthropathy are
best understood in terms of the Eichenholtz classification.
Stage 0 (acute): normal radiographs
Stage I (fragmentation): osteopenia, periarticular fragmentation, subluxation
Stage II (coalescence): absorption of debris, early fusion, and sclerosis
Stage III (reconstruction): joint arthrosis, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis, deformity


Plain Radiography
In Eichenholtz stage 0, plain radiographs appear normal, representing the acute phase of
the disease before substantial arthropathy or osteopenia has occurred1,10,11 (Table 1).
In stage I, radiographs demonstrate osteopenia, periarticular fragmentation, and joint
subluxation or dislocation (Figure 1, A and B; Resource 2). In stage II, radiographs
demonstrate absorption of debris, fusion of bony fragments, and early bony sclerosis
(Figure 1, C). Finally, in stage III, radiographs demonstrate osteophytes, complete joint
obliteration, and extensive subchondral sclerosis (Figure 1, D). Deformity can occur
during stage I to stage III and may be intra-articular or extra-articular in origin.
Figure 1 Lateral foot radiographs demonstrate the progression of Brodsky type 1
Charcot neuroarthropathy of the foot through the Eichenholtz stages. A rocker-bottom
deformity developed. A, In stage 0 or early stage I, no evidence of fragmentation or
osteopenia is present. B, In late stage I, fragmentation of bone is observed around the
Lisfranc joint (arrow). C, In stage II, bone debris begins to resorb and consolidate. D,
Stage III involves further consolidation and remodeling of fracture fragments, with
increasing bony sclerosis. (Reproduced from van der Ven A, Chapman CB, Bowker JH:
Charcot neuroarthropathy of the foot and ankle. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2009;17[9]:562-
571.)
Advanced Imaging Studies

The primary indication for advanced imaging studies in patients in whom Charcot arthropathy
is suspected involves differentiating Charcot arthropathy from infection.
MRI and nuclear medicine may be useful.
Three-phase technetium-99m scintigraphy in combination with indium-111–labeled leukocyte
scintigraphy is best for differentiating Charcot arthropathy from osteomyelitis.
MRI is best for differentiating Charcot arthropathy from soft-tissue abscess.

Advanced Imaging Studies
Signs of Charcot arthropathy, soft-tissue infection, and osteomyelitis may overlap
substantially, particularly in patients with an adjacent soft-tissue defect. Physical
examination and laboratory signs of infection, such as fever, leukocytosis, increased
blood glucose level, greater insulin requirement, and nondependent nature of erythema
and swelling, may help establish the diagnosis but may not be definitive. Plain
radiography has been shown to be 50% specific in detecting osteomyelitis.13 Although
plain radiography is a critical imaging modality in characterizing deformity and the
Eichenholtz stage of Charcot arthropathy, it is not ideal for ruling out infection. If
superimposed osteomyelitis or soft-tissue abscess is suspected, advanced imaging
studies may be helpful. MRI and bone scintigraphy are options for advanced imaging.
Three-phase technetium-99m scintigraphy in combination with indium-111–labeled
leukocyte scintigraphy is associated with a sensitivity of 93% to 100% and a specificity of
approximately 80%.1,14,15 Studies suggest that MRI is less specific than the combination
of three-phase technetium-99m scintigraphy and indium-111–labeled leukocyte
scintigraphy in detecting osteomyelitis;16 however, MRI, with its excellent soft-tissue
resolution, is superior to bone scanning in ruling out associated soft-tissue abscess.
Classification
The Eichenholtz classification provides staging in terms of patient history, physical examination
findings, and imaging study findings.
This classification system also guides management.
Brodsky created an anatomic classification system for Charcot arthropathy.

Type 1 involves the midfoot and accounts for approximately 60% of Charcot arthropathy.
Type 2 involves the hindfoot and accounts for 30% to 35% of Charcot arthropathy.
Type 3 involves the tibiotalar joint or calcaneal tuberosity and accounts for the remaining 5%
to 10% of Charcot arthropathy

Classification
Although the Eichenholtz classification provides staging in terms of patient history,
physical examination findings, and imaging study findings (Table 1), it does not
differentiate in terms of anatomy.1,10,11 Brodsky characterized Charcot arthropathy
based on anatomic location throughout the foot and ankle12 (Figure 2). In this system,
type 1 arthropathy occurs at the tarsometatarsal joint. This joint was the most common
location of Charcot arthropathy, accounting for 60% of cases. In type 1 arthropathy,
collapse tends to lead to a fixed rocker-bottom deformity with valgus angulation through
the midfoot. As a result, patients with type 1 arthropathy have bony exostoses on the
plantar aspect of the foot, which become sources of recurrent ulceration. In type 2
arthropathy, the subtalar and Chopart joints are affected individually or together. This
type of arthropathy accounts for 10% of cases. The deformity that arises from type 2
arthropathy often is unstable and requires prolonged immobilization. In type 3A
arthropathy, the tibiotalar joint is affected. Deformity tends to be varus or valgus
collapse, which leads to recurrent ulceration and osteomyelitis over the malleoli. In type
3B deformity, fracture occurs at the calcaneal tuberosity, and proximal migration of the
tuberosity may occur.

RA, Saltzman CL, eds: Surgery of the Foot and Ankle, ed 8. St. Louis, MO, Mosby, 2006, p
1341.)
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Most patients with Charcot arthropathy are initially treated nonsurgically, particularly those
with Eichenholtz stage 0 or stage I.
The goals of management for Charcot arthropathy are a plantigrade, stable foot that can fit
into a shoe and the absence of recurrent ulceration.
Total contact casting (TCC) and a Charcot restraint orthotic walker are the mainstays of
management.
Most patients with acute Charcot arthropathy can be treated effectively via pressure-
relieving methods, such as TCC, the benchmark of management.

10/24

TCC permits an even distribution of foot pressures across the plantar surface of the foot.
TCC with guarded ambulation yields a mean healing rate of 75%.
Casts are changed every 2 to 4 weeks until erythema and edema resolve, the temperature of
the affected limb diminishes, and radiographs demonstrate stabilization, representing
progress through the Eichenholtz stages.
TCC commonly is continued for as long as 4 months.
If the active disease phase has ended, the patient is fitted with a Charcot restraint orthotic
walker and, later, ideally with custom shoes and/or orthoses.

Techniques/Procedures
The goal of treatment for a patient with Charcot arthropathy of the foot and ankle is a
stable, plantigrade foot that can fit into a shoe and facilitate ambulation without
recurrent ulceration.1 In most patients, this goal can be achieved via nonsurgical
treatment.17 The mainstay of management in the unstable (early) phases of Charcot
arthropathy is immobilization and non–weight bearing in TCC18-20 (Figure 3). All bony
prominences are padded with the use of felt or foam, and the entire ankle and foot is
encased to distribute loads. Settling within the cast may lead to instability and ulceration;
therefore, cast changes must occur frequently, typically every 2 to 4 weeks.

In Eichenholtz stage I Charcot arthropathy, the TCC is maintained until the surgeon
thinks that all involved joints are prepared to sustain physiologic stress, typically
approximately 2 to 4 months.1,18-20 Indicators of improvement include radiographic

resolution of fragmentation and a decrease in skin temperature. For patients who are in
or progress to Eichenholtz stage II, TCC remains a treatment option; however, a molded
total-contact polypropylene ankle-foot orthosis (Charcot restraint orthotic walker) often
is a more convenient option21 (Figure 4). This orthosis typically consists of a two-piece
rigid clamshell with a rocker-bottom and a custom-molded removable insole, and it
facilitates continued immobilization but imposes fewer restrictions than TCC. Eichenholtz
stage III Charcot arthropathy is managed via custom accommodative shoes and inserts,
which often can be funded via the Medicare benefit covering therapeutic shoes for
patients with diabetes mellitus, to prevent recurrence and ulceration.
Reviews of outcomes after TCC reveal high rates of progression to therapeutic footwear
after several months without the need for surgical management.18-20 However, orthosis
use and weight-bearing compliance rates are poor, and complications, such as ulcers
requiring local wound care, are common.

Surgical Management
Indications
Skin breakdown because of equinus deformity or focal prominences that do not resolve with
brace management or TCC
Severe deformity that cannot be managed with use of a brace
Unsuccessful previous surgical management
Recurrent infection or infection not successfully managed via nonsurgical treatment
Acute surgical correction
Limited indications exist for stabilization of a joint in the early Eichenholtz stages of Charcot
arthropathy.
Surgical management performed in the early Eichenholtz stages results in high rates of
nonunion, infection, wound complications, late deformity, and eventual amputation.
The more proximal the deformity, the more difficult stabilization via cast immobilization or
brace management; such Charcot joints are most likely to benefit from early reconstruction.
Late surgical correction
If Eichenholtz stage II or stage III is achieved and deformity persists, the surgeon must decide
whether accommodative, nonsurgical management via a combination of inlay-depth shoes,
foot orthoses, and ankle-foot orthoses is adequate to meet the long-term goals of the
patient.
If a plantigrade weight-bearing surface cannot be achieved, surgical reconstruction is best
performed during Eichenholtz stage III, after the inflammatory process has resolved.
Indications for surgical management of Charcot arthropathy of the foot include recurrent
ulcers and instability or deformity not controlled by a brace.
Surgical treatment options are exostectomy or reconstruction with osteotomy and
arthrodesis.
Surgical treatment may be indicated in as many as 50% of patients.
Exostectomy can be performed to excise bony prominences that cause ulcers, most
commonly on the plantar midfoot in patients with Brodsky type 1 disease.
Reconstruction via osteotomy and arthrodesis may be considered for correction of fixed
deformity and severe instability that precludes successful brace management.

Postoperative infectious complications are common.
Patients with complicated diabetes mellitus may have union rates as low as 50%.
Deformity correction during osteotomy and arthrodesis is achieved via internal fixation
and/or thin-wire external fixation.

Surgical Management
In general, surgical correction of deformity is delayed until Eichenholtz stage III to
increase the likelihood of success and decrease the rates of nonunion, infection, wound
complications, late deformity, and amputation.1 In patients with ulceration after
unsuccessful nonsurgical management, simple exostectomy of the bony prominence
deep to the ulcer is an excellent treatment option.22 In patients with midfoot Charcot
arthropathy, these prominences are not new bone but are tarsal bones that have shifted
to a nonanatomic (commonly plantar) position. If exostectomy is followed by protective
brace management, limb-salvage rates may be as high as 90%; however, one or more
revision procedures may be required. Exostectomy is most commonly performed for the
management of Brodsky type 1 (tarsometatarsal) deformity, in which a plantar collapse
of the arch exposes the skin plantar to the navicular, cuneiforms, and cuboid to atypical
loads.
In patients with more severe and more proximal deformity, simple exostectomy often is
inadequate, and arthrodesis commonly becomes the only deformity-correction option to
avoid amputation. Arthrodesis most commonly is achieved via meticulous joint
preparation and internal fixation, including screws, pins, plates, and/or intramedullary
beaming23 (Figure 5). Occasionally, staged procedures are required in patients with
concurrent infection. Osteotomies commonly are required to achieve a plantigrade foot
and often may involve large wedge resections, including resection of proximal and distal
articular surfaces, doubling as preparation for arthrodesis. Intramedullary
tibiotalocalcaneal fixation is an excellent treatment option for patients with Brodsky type
2 or type 3 deformity24,25 (Figure 6). Arthrodesis typically is achieved by 11 to 22 weeks
postoperatively, requiring extended immobilization and non–weight bearing for 3
months postoperatively.26,27

Deformity correction via external fixation or combined internal and external fixation
recently has become popular28,29 (Figure 7). This option may be a less invasive
treatment modality with the advantages of single-stage management, even in the
presence of infection or ulceration; access for soft-tissue monitoring; and immediate
postoperative weight bearing via sleds on the bottom of the thin-wire frame. Large
deformities can be corrected and stabilized via osteotomies with or without more limited
internal fixation, in comparison to techniques without an external fixator.

to center the corrected foot within the preassembled external ring fixator. B, Two or

two rings. (Reproduced with permission from Pinzur MS: Neutral ring fixation for high-

Complication rates of internal fixation alone are as high as 70%, including fracture,
recurrent ulceration, hardware malpositioning, and infection.23-25,30 However,
plantigrade, braceable feet generally are achieved, with amputation rates as low as zero

to 10% at a follow-up ranging from 1 to 4 years.24,31 Stable fibrous union rather than
true bony union is common and generally leads to an acceptable result with effective
brace management and close soft-tissue monitoring.
Results of external fixation are similar, with limb salvage rates higher than 90% despite
the particularly complicated patient population selected for this treatment protocol.28,29
Compared with internal fixation alone, recurrent ulceration is rare; however, pin tract
infection is common.
Limb amputation is reserved for patients in whom reconstruction failed, resulting in
unstable arthrodesis and/or recurrent infection or ulceration.32,33 The decision to
perform amputation is related to not only the condition of the limb but also the general
health and functional status of the patient. Amputation generally is performed below the
knee, at the transtibial level (Videos 1 and 2).
